# Results — Study 891 (Insurance Float Engine)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — a broad
P&C-insurer basket is a **structural** money-machine: the "float" (premiums held before claims)
compounds like near-zero-cost leverage, so the basket should deliver a genuine **risk-adjusted
edge over the market** attributable to the float structure, not merely to financial-sector beta.
Tested on **KIE** (SPDR S&P Insurance, equal-weight), **IAK** (iShares U.S. Insurance) vs
**SPY**, both legs measured excess-of-cash (minus **BIL**), with **KBE** (SPDR S&P Bank) as the
financial-sector control. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py`
to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial
current month is dropped). Fingerprint `3a54dbc09ab6`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily **total-return** closes: KIE, IAK, SPY, KBE, BIL — public, no key |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-06-30 daily; **229** complete months **2007-06 → 2026-06** (BIL, the cash leg, binds the common start); as-of 2026-06-30 |
| Cash leg | **BIL** (SPDR 1-3 Month T-Bill ETF) total return — every Sharpe is excess-of-cash so a rising short rate can't flatter a thin edge; BIL's ~0.14 % ER makes it a tradable, conservative cash proxy |
| Inference | **Newey-West HAC *t*** (6 lags) on the monthly return difference and on all regression coefficients; a circular-block bootstrap 95 % CI on each excess Sharpe |
| Decomposition | CAPM (insurer excess on market excess) and a two-factor (market + **bank − market** spread) regression — the decisive "is it float or financial beta?" test |
| Execution / costs | rotation probe uses the *prior* 12-month insurer-vs-market lead (one-month lag); isolation trade pays 40 bps/yr borrow on the short leg + 5 bps one-way × ~1 rebalance/yr |

> **Survivorship / short-history note (Signal axis).** All five ETFs are live survivors and the
> insurer wrappers are young by structural-premium standards (KIE/IAK list 2005-06; the common
> BIL-anchored sample is only **19 years, one of which is the GFC**). The *effect* is a basket
> property, not a cross-sectional stock pick, so survivorship bias is mild — but the honest
> caveat is that 19 years spanning one financial crisis is a short tape on which to certify a
> "structural" premium either way.

## Descriptives — the basket *lost* to the market, and it is *more* volatile

| basket | CAGR | ann vol | excess Sharpe | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **KIE** (insurers, EW) | +7.86 % | 21.73 % | **+0.398** | **−69.7 %** |
| IAK (insurers, CW) | +6.80 % | 20.85 % | +0.359 | −72.2 % |
| **SPY** (market) | **+10.68 %** | **15.58 %** | **+0.644** | −50.8 % |
| KBE (banks, EW) | +3.21 % | 27.64 % | +0.209 | −76.6 % |

The insurer baskets compounded **below** the market at **higher** volatility and a **deeper**
drawdown. The float-engine folklore predicts the opposite.

## The race — excess-vs-excess Sharpe advantage is *negative*, and insignificant

Both legs excess-of-cash (minus BIL). "Advantage" = insurer Sharpe − market Sharpe (the
folklore predicts > 0). "diff" is the monthly (insurer − market) return; its HAC *t* is the
honest significance of the out/under-performance.

| pair | n | excess Sharpe | SPY excess Sharpe | **advantage** | insurer − SPY | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| KIE vs SPY | 229 | +0.398 | +0.644 | **−0.246** | −1.39 %/yr | **−0.49** |
| IAK vs SPY | 229 | +0.359 | +0.644 | −0.285 | −2.56 %/yr | −0.90 |

The advantage is negative and the return difference is statistically zero (|*t*| < 1). There is
no risk-adjusted edge over the market to certify — if anything the sign runs the wrong way.

## Bootstrap Sharpe CI — you cannot even separate the insurer Sharpe from zero

Circular-block bootstrap (2000 draws), 95 % CI on the excess Sharpe.

| basket | excess Sharpe | 95 % CI | P(Sharpe < 0) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| KIE | +0.398 | [−0.060, +0.966] | 0.04 |
| IAK | +0.359 | [−0.116, +0.949] | 0.07 |
| **SPY** | +0.644 | **[+0.180, +1.182]** | 0.00 |
| KBE | +0.209 | [−0.231, +0.734] | 0.17 |

SPY's interval clears zero; the insurer intervals *include* zero and sit almost entirely below
SPY's point estimate. The market's Sharpe is the only one you can bank.

## CAPM — no alpha over the market (negative, insignificant)

`insurer_ex = α + β·market_ex`, Newey-West errors.

| basket | α (%/yr) | HAC *t* | β | *t*(β vs 1) | R² |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| KIE | **−2.48** | −0.84 | 1.109 | +0.87 | 0.632 |
| IAK | −3.10 | −0.95 | 1.053 | +0.46 | 0.619 |

The insurer basket carries slightly *more* than one unit of market beta and delivers a
**negative** alpha that is indistinguishable from zero. No float premium survives the market.

## The decisive test — it's financial-sector beta, not float

`insurer_ex = α + β·market_ex + s·(bank_ex − market_ex)`. The bank-minus-market spread is a
clean financial-sector factor. If the "float premium" were real it would survive as a positive
`α`; if it is just sector beta, the bank factor soaks it up and `α` collapses.

| basket | α (%/yr) | HAC *t* | β(market) | load(bank spread) | HAC *t* | R² |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **KIE** | **−0.11** | **−0.04** | 1.024 | **+0.357** | **+6.27** | 0.738 |
| IAK | −0.96 | −0.34 | 0.977 | +0.322 | +5.81 | 0.712 |

Adding one financial-sector factor drives the insurer alpha to **exactly zero** (−0.11 %/yr,
*t* = −0.04) while the bank-spread loading is large and hugely significant (+0.36, *t* = 6.3).
**The insurer basket *is* a financial-sector-beta vehicle.** Whatever the float does inside the
firms, at the traded-basket level it shows up as sector risk, not as a distinct premium.

## Era cut — the deficit is not a one-crisis artefact

Excess Sharpe by era (KIE the headline basket).

| era | n | KIE | SPY | KBE | KIE − SPY advantage |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GFC 2007-09 | 31 | −0.329 | −0.447 | −0.647 | **+0.118** |
| 2010-15 | 72 | +0.872 | +0.996 | +0.576 | −0.125 |
| 2016-20 | 60 | +0.564 | +0.938 | +0.336 | −0.374 |
| 2021-26 | 66 | +0.633 | +0.789 | +0.462 | −0.157 |
| **post-GFC 2010+** | 198 | +0.700 | +0.907 | +0.448 | **−0.207** |

The **only** era the insurer basket out-Sharpes the market is the **2007-09 crash** (it fell a
bit less — a defensive-in-a-panic property), and only by +0.12. In every calm era it *trails*
the market, and it trails across all of post-GFC 2010+. A structural edge would show up in the
calm, not just the crash.

## One real, *different* finding — insurers beat banks (but not cleanly)

Insurer minus bank (KBE) monthly return — a *within-financials* claim, **not** an edge over the
market:

| pair | mean | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| KIE − KBE | +2.89 %/yr | +0.96 |
| IAK − KBE | +1.71 %/yr | +0.58 |

Float-funded insurers did ride a better path than spread-levered banks (KBE's Sharpe 0.21,
drawdown −77 %), consistent with the economics — but even this within-sector gap does not clear
*t* ≥ 2 on 19 years, and it is a different claim from the one the folklore makes.

## Tradability — nothing to pocket over the market

**(a) One-month-lag rotation** (own KIE when it has beaten SPY over the trailing 12 months, else
SPY; 5 bps one-way per switch): net **+9.51 %/yr** (excess Sharpe +0.490) vs **always-SPY
+11.41 %/yr** and always-KIE +10.03 %/yr, 30 switches, KIE held 47 % of the time. The timing rule
underperforms simply owning the market.

**(b) Isolation trade** (long KIE / short SPY, dollar-neutral; 40 bps/yr borrow on the short leg
+ 5 bps one-way × ~1 rebalance/yr = 0.50 %/yr charge):

| leg | annual | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| gross | −1.39 %/yr | −0.49 |
| **net** | **−1.89 %/yr** | **−0.66** |

The trade that would monetise a float premium over the market *loses* money before costs and
loses more after. There is no bankable edge here — the apparent "engine" is financial-sector
beta you can rent more cheaply and less riskily by just holding the market.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is faithful *(never market evidence)*

Deterministic world (`synthetic_world`, seed 891): insurer excess = planted edge + market beta
+ a bank-spread loading + idiosyncratic noise.

| planted edge | Sharpe advantage | CAPM α (HAC *t*) | two-factor α (HAC *t*) | bank load (*t*) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 %/yr (null) | +0.092 | +2.07 %/yr (**+1.48**) | +1.87 %/yr (+1.40) | +0.387 (+10.70) |
| +4 %/yr | +0.305 | +6.07 %/yr (**+4.34**) | +5.87 %/yr (+4.40) | +0.387 (+10.70) |

The zero-edge null does not fire (the CAPM *t* stays under 2 even though the planted bank beta
adds a ~2 %/yr *apparent* alpha — exactly the confound the two-factor test is built to strip); a
planted +4 %/yr edge is recovered with *t* > 4 and survives the bank control. The estimator is
unbiased — so the real-tape verdict (alpha → 0 once the sector factor is added) is the genuine
article, not a machinery artefact.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** The claimed *edge over the market attributable to float* is **absent, and
  the sign runs the wrong way.** KIE/IAK excess Sharpe (0.40 / 0.36) trails SPY (0.64); the
  Sharpe advantage is **−0.25 / −0.29** with the return difference statistically zero (HAC
  *t* = −0.49 / −0.90); CAPM alpha is **−2.5 / −3.1 %/yr** (*t* < 1); and the decisive
  two-factor test collapses the insurer alpha to **−0.11 %/yr (*t* = −0.04)** against a large,
  significant financial-sector loading (+0.36, *t* = 6.3). The advantage is negative in every
  calm era; the bootstrap can't even separate the insurer Sharpe from zero. The float is real
  economics, but at the traded-basket level it *is* financial-sector beta — not a distinct,
  market-beating premium. (The one honest positive — insurers out-Sharpe banks by +2.9 %/yr — is
  a within-financials point at *t* = 0.96, a different claim, not clean.) Named on this axis:
  19-year sample, one crisis inside it.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is no positive net edge to harvest over the market. The
  long-insurer/short-market isolation trade is **−1.4 %/yr gross, −1.9 %/yr net**; the
  one-month-lag rotation nets **+9.5 %/yr, below always-SPY's +11.4 %/yr**. A hidden
  financial-sector beta explains all of the apparent sector performance, and you can rent that
  beta more cheaply — and at a shallower drawdown — by simply owning SPY.
